column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: What is DNA replication?
column14: Making an RNA copy of one gene
column15: Making an exact copy of a cell's DNA
column16: Breaking DNA down into nucleotides for energy
column17: Joining the DNA from two parents into one molecule
column28: Replication copies all of the cell's DNA so there are two identical molecules. Making an RNA copy of one gene is transcription, which is the most common mix-up.
column29: Think about what the word replicate means in everyday life, like a replica of a famous painting.

column9: During which part of the cell cycle does a cell copy its DNA?
column14: S phase of interphase
column15: Prophase of mitosis
column16: Anaphase of mitosis
column17: Cytokinesis
column28: DNA is copied during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, before mitosis starts. A common mistake is picking a stage of mitosis, but by then the chromosomes are already doubled.
column29: The copying has to be finished while the cell is still growing and getting ready, before any dividing begins.

column9: In a cell from a maple leaf, where are the chromosomes copied?
column14: On the ribosomes
column15: In the cell membrane
column16: In the central vacuole
column17: In the nucleus
column28: Plant and animal cells keep their chromosomes in the nucleus, so that is where they are copied. Ribosomes make proteins, not DNA, which is a common mix-up.
column29: Where does a eukaryotic cell keep its chromosomes?

column9: In a classroom model of replication, one student slides along the DNA ladder and pulls the two sides apart. Which enzyme is that student acting out?
column14: DNA polymerase
column15: DNA ligase
column16: Helicase
column17: Amylase
column28: Helicase separates (unzips) the two strands. DNA polymerase builds the new strands after they are apart, and mixing up those two jobs is the common mistake. Amylase digests starch and has nothing to do with DNA.
column29: This enzyme's job comes first, before any new bases can be added.

column9: Which enzyme adds new nucleotides, one at a time, to build a new DNA strand?
column14: Helicase
column15: DNA polymerase
column16: DNA ligase
column17: Lipase
column28: DNA polymerase reads the old strand and adds matching nucleotides to build the new one. Helicase only unzips and ligase only seals gaps, so choosing them is the usual mistake.
column29: Poly- means many. This enzyme strings many nucleotides together.

column9: In DNA, adenine (A) always pairs with which base?
column14: Thymine (T)
column15: Guanine (G)
column16: Cytosine (C)
column17: Uracil (U)
column28: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. Uracil is a common wrong answer: U is found only in RNA, never in DNA.
column29: One pair is A with ___ and the other pair is C with G.

column9: During replication, DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide with cytosine (C). Which base must be on the old strand across from it?
column14: Adenine (A)
column15: Thymine (T)
column16: Uracil (U)
column17: Guanine (G)
column28: Cytosine always pairs with guanine, so the old strand must have a G at that spot. Picking T mixes up the two pairs.
column29: Recall the base pairing rule: which base is cytosine's only partner?

column9: When DNA polymerase reaches a T on the template strand, it adds a nucleotide with the base ___.
column28: T pairs with A, so the new strand gets adenine. Typing U is the common mistake: U is an RNA base and never goes into DNA.
column29: T and its partner are one of the two base pairs in DNA.

column9: A short piece of a template strand reads CAT. Type the new strand that DNA polymerase builds on it. New strand: ___
column28: C pairs with G, A with T, and T with A, so the new strand is GTA. Copying the same letters (CAT) is the common mistake: the new strand is complementary, not identical, to its template.
column29: Go one base at a time and write each base's partner.

column9: A lab card shows a template strand: GACT. Type the new DNA strand that will be built on it. New strand: ___
column20: CTGA|C T G A|C-T-G-A|C,T,G,A|C, T, G, A
column28: G→C, A→T, C→G, T→A gives CTGA. A common mistake is writing U across from A, but new DNA uses T.
column29: Match each base with its partner: A with T, C with G.

column9: Part of a gene in a corn plant has the template strand TTGCA. Type the new strand that forms during replication. New strand: ___
column20: AACGT|A A C G T|A-A-C-G-T|A,A,C,G,T|A, A, C, G, T
column28: T→A, T→A, G→C, C→G, A→T gives AACGT. Mixing up which bases pair (for example putting G across from T) is the common mistake.
column29: Write the partner of each base in the same order.

column9: A template strand reads ACGTT. Which new strand will DNA polymerase build on it?
column14: UGCAA
column15: ACGTT
column16: TGCAA
column17: TGCAT
column28: A→T, C→G, G→C, T→A, T→A gives TGCAA. UGCAA uses an RNA base, ACGTT just copies the template, and TGCAT gets the last base wrong.
column29: Pair each base on the template one at a time, and remember which base DNA uses instead of U.

column9: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative. What does that mean?
column14: One new molecule keeps both original strands and the other gets two new strands
column15: Each new DNA molecule has one original strand and one newly built strand
column16: Every strand is a patchwork of old and new pieces mixed together
column17: Only half of the cell's DNA gets copied
column28: Semi means half and conservative means saved, so each new molecule saves half (one strand) of the original. Thinking one copy is all old and the other all new is the common mistake.
column29: Break the word apart: semi = half, conserve = save.

column9: In DNA replication, what is the template?
column14: An old strand that is used as the pattern for building a new strand
column15: The enzyme that glues the short pieces of new DNA together into one strand
column16: The sugar found in each nucleotide
column17: The finished copy of the DNA molecule
column28: Each old strand is a template: its bases tell polymerase which bases to add. Calling the finished copy the template is the common mix-up; the template is the pattern, not the product.
column29: A template is like a stencil or pattern you trace from.

column9: Why must a skin cell copy its DNA before it divides?
column14: So the cell can make more energy
column15: So the cell can get rid of its old DNA
column16: So each new cell ends up with twice as much DNA as the parent cell
column17: So each new cell gets a complete set of DNA
column28: Copying the DNA first means both new cells get a full, identical set of instructions. Twice the DNA is the common mistake: the copies are split up, so each new cell has the same amount the parent started with.
column29: Think about what each of the two new cells needs in order to work.

column9: To separate the two strands of DNA, helicase breaks which bonds?
column14: The bonds between sugars and phosphates in the backbone
column15: The bonds inside each base
column16: The hydrogen bonds between the paired bases
column17: The peptide bonds between amino acids
column28: Helicase breaks the weak hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together, so the strands come apart like a zipper. The sugar-phosphate backbone stays whole, which is a common mistake. Peptide bonds are in proteins, not DNA.
column29: Think about where the two strands are attached to each other: the sides of the ladder or the middle of the rungs?

column9: What are the building blocks that DNA polymerase adds to a growing DNA strand?
column14: Amino acids
column15: Nucleotides
column16: Glucose molecules
column17: Fatty acids
column28: DNA is a nucleic acid, and its building blocks are nucleotides. Amino acids build proteins, which is the most common mix-up.
column29: Each building block has a phosphate, a sugar and a base.

column9: A free nucleotide waiting to be added to a new DNA strand is made of which three parts? Select all that apply.
column14: Ribose sugar
column15: Phosphate group
column16: Fatty acid
column17: Amino acid
column28: A DNA nucleotide has a phosphate group, the sugar deoxyribose and a nitrogen base. Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides, which is the common mistake.
column29: The D in DNA stands for the sugar's name.

column9: A newly built DNA strand has gaps between short pieces, like train cars that are not hooked together yet. Which enzyme connects the pieces?
column14: DNA ligase
column15: Helicase
column16: DNA polymerase
column17: Lactase
column28: DNA ligase seals the gaps, joining short pieces into one continuous strand. Polymerase builds the pieces but does not join them, which is the common mix-up.
column29: This enzyme's name comes from a Latin word meaning to tie or bind.

column9: Which of these is NOT used to build a new DNA strand?
column14: Deoxyribose
column15: Phosphate
column16: Thymine
column17: Uracil
column28: Uracil is an RNA base, so it is never used in DNA. Deoxyribose, phosphate and thymine are all parts of DNA nucleotides. Students often add U because they are thinking of transcription.
column29: One of these belongs to RNA, not DNA.

column9: One DNA molecule goes through one round of replication. How many DNA molecules are there when it is finished? (Enter a number.)
column28: One molecule is copied into two identical molecules. Answering 4 is a common mistake that counts strands instead of molecules.
column29: Replication turns one molecule into how many copies of it?

column9: When DNA is replicated, uracil (U) is added across from adenine (A) on the template strand.
column28: False. Uracil is only in RNA. In DNA replication, thymine (T) is added across from adenine.
column29: Which molecule uses U: DNA or RNA?

column9: How does the base sequence of the two new DNA molecules compare with the original molecule?
column14: Each new molecule has only half of the original genes
column15: One new molecule has the original sequence and the other has a new one
column16: Both new molecules have the same base sequence as the original
column17: Both new molecules have completely different sequences
column28: Base pairing makes each new molecule an exact copy of the original. A common mistake is thinking the genes get split in half, but the full sequence is copied into both.
column29: If each base can pair with only one partner, can the copy turn out differently?

column9: Match each part of DNA replication to its job.
column14: Helicase :: Unzips the double helix by separating the two strands
column15: DNA polymerase :: Adds matching nucleotides to build a new strand
column16: DNA ligase :: Seals short pieces of new DNA into one strand
column17: Template strand :: Old strand whose bases are the pattern for the new strand
column28: Helicase unzips, DNA polymerase builds, ligase seals, and each old strand is the template. Mixing up helicase and polymerase is the most common mistake.
column29: Put the enzymes in the order they act: unzip first, then build, then seal.

column9: The two strands of DNA are called complementary. What does complementary mean here?
column14: The two strands have exactly the same bases in the same order
column15: Each base pairs only with its partner: A with T and C with G
column16: Any base can pair with any other base
column17: The strands are made of protein
column28: Complementary means the strands fit together because each base has one partner. Thinking the strands are identical is the common mistake; they are matching partners, not copies of each other.
column29: Think of puzzle pieces that only fit one specific neighbor.

column9: A zipper is often used as a model for DNA. Which part of replication does pulling the zipper open stand for?
column14: Helicase separating the two strands
column15: DNA polymerase checking for mistakes
column16: DNA ligase gluing pieces together
column17: The cell splitting into two cells
column28: Opening the zipper is like helicase breaking the hydrogen bonds and separating the strands. The cell splitting is a common wrong pick, but that happens later, during cell division.
column29: Opening the zipper is the very first step. Which enzyme acts first?

column9: DNA polymerase has just added a G across from a T on the template strand. What does it usually do next?
column14: Leaves the G in place, because any base can pair with the T on the template
column15: Stops replication for the rest of the cell's life
column16: Changes the G into a U
column17: Removes the wrong base and replaces it with the correct one
column28: DNA polymerase proofreads its work and fixes most wrong bases (T should pair with A). Thinking any base works is the common mistake; only the correct partner keeps the copy accurate.
column29: Polymerase checks its own work, a bit like a student rereading an essay.

column9: Before one bacterium splits into two by binary fission, what must happen to its DNA?
column14: It is cut in half so each new bacterium gets half of the genes it needs
column15: It is changed into RNA
column16: It is copied so each new bacterium gets a full copy
column17: It is destroyed and rebuilt from scratch in each new cell after the split
column28: Bacteria replicate their DNA before dividing so both new cells get a complete set. Cutting the DNA in half is the common mistake; each new cell would then be missing genes.
column29: Each new bacterium has to be able to live on its own.

column9: The enzyme that reads the template strand and builds the new strand is DNA ___.
column28: DNA polymerase builds the new strand by adding matching nucleotides. Writing helicase is the common mistake: helicase only unzips.
column29: Its name starts with poly-, meaning many.

column9: Which event must happen FIRST in DNA replication?
column14: DNA ligase seals the gaps between pieces
column15: The two strands are separated
column16: DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides
column17: Two identical DNA molecules twist back into helices
column28: The strands must come apart before polymerase can read the bases. A common mistake is starting with polymerase, but the bases are hidden inside the helix until it opens.
column29: Can you read the bases while they are still paired up inside the helix?

column9: Put the main steps of DNA replication in order.
column14: DNA polymerase adds matching nucleotides along each old strand
column15: Two identical DNA molecules are finished, each with one old and one new strand
column16: DNA ligase seals the gaps between short pieces of new DNA
column17: Helicase separates the two strands
column28: Unzip → build → seal → two finished molecules. The common mistake is putting ligase before polymerase, but ligase can only seal pieces that have already been built.
column29: Something has to be built before it can be glued together.

column9: Which base pair could be found in a correctly copied DNA molecule?
column14: G–C
column15: A–G
column16: C–T
column17: A–U
column28: The only DNA pairs are A–T and G–C. A–U is a common wrong choice because it happens in RNA, not DNA.
column29: Use the rule: A with T, C with G.

column9: Select every base pair that could appear in a newly copied DNA molecule. Select all that apply.
column14: C–G
column15: A–U
column16: G–A
column17: A–T
column28: A–T, C–G and T–A all follow the pairing rule (T–A is just A–T written the other way). A–U is the common mistake because it belongs to RNA. G–T and G–A break the rule.
column29: The order of the letters in a pair doesn't matter. Only the partners do.

column9: Where do the nucleotides that build the new DNA strands come from?
column14: They are cut off the old strands
column15: Ribosomes make them at the replication site
column16: They come from the cell membrane
column17: A supply of free nucleotides in the nucleus
column28: The cell keeps a supply of free nucleotides, and polymerase picks matching ones to add. Thinking the bases are cut off the old strands is the common mistake; the old strands stay whole and act as templates.
column29: The old strands have to stay whole so they can be the pattern.

column9: During replication, both strands of the original DNA molecule are used as templates.
column28: True. The two strands separate and each one is the pattern for a new partner strand, which is how one molecule becomes two. Thinking only one strand gets copied is the common mistake.
column29: Count how many new strands are built to make two complete molecules.

column9: How many strands does one DNA molecule have before replication starts?
column28: DNA is a double helix, so it has 2 strands. 46 is a common wrong pick, but that is the number of chromosomes in a human body cell, not the strands in one molecule.
column29: DNA is called a double helix.

column9: A student writes the new strand for the template AGC as UCG. What mistake did the student make?
column14: Should have copied the template exactly, so the new strand should read AGC
column15: Used U, which is an RNA base; the new DNA strand should be TCG
column16: Should have written the strand backwards: GCU
column17: No mistake; UCG is correct
column28: DNA uses T, not U, so the correct new strand is TCG. Copying the template exactly is another common mistake, since the new strand is complementary.
column29: Which molecule uses U as a base?

column9: The bonds that hold the base pairs together are much weaker than the bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone. Why is that helpful during replication?
column14: The strands can be pulled apart easily for copying without breaking the backbone
column15: It makes DNA dissolve in water
column16: It lets each base switch to any partner it wants
column17: It makes the sugar-phosphate backbone stronger, so the strands never come apart during copying
column28: Weak bonds in the middle let helicase open the strands without breaking the backbone. Thinking weak bonds let bases switch partners is the common mistake; the pairing rule still holds.
column29: A zipper is useful because it opens easily but stays shut when you need it to.

column9: In a DNA model lab, the template strand is built with the beads G, G, C, T, A. Type the bases on the new strand in the same order. New strand: ___
column20: CCGAT|C C G A T|C-C-G-A-T|C,C,G,A,T|C, C, G, A, T
column28: G→C, G→C, C→G, T→A, A→T gives CCGAT. A common mistake is pairing G with T or putting U across from A.
column29: Go bead by bead and write each partner.

column9: In DNA, cytosine always pairs with ___.
column28: Cytosine pairs with guanine, and adenine pairs with thymine. Answering T is the common mix-up of the two pairs.
column29: The two pairs are A–T and C–?

column9: A human liver cell is about to divide. Which statement about its DNA is true just before mitosis starts?
column14: Its DNA will be copied during anaphase
column15: Its DNA will be copied after the cell splits
column16: Liver cells never copy their DNA
column17: Its DNA has already been copied during S phase
column28: DNA is copied in S phase, before mitosis begins. Thinking it is copied during mitosis is the common mistake; mitosis only separates copies that already exist.
column29: Interphase comes before mitosis. Which part of interphase is for copying?

column9: Which of these is an enzyme that helps copy DNA?
column14: Hemoglobin
column15: Cellulose
column16: DNA polymerase
column17: Cholesterol
column28: DNA polymerase is the enzyme that builds new DNA strands. Hemoglobin carries oxygen, cellulose is plant fiber and cholesterol is a lipid, so none of them copy DNA.
column29: Most enzyme names end in -ase.

column9: A short DNA molecule has 10 base pairs. After one round of replication, how many base pairs does EACH new molecule have?
column28: Each new molecule is a full copy, so each has 10 base pairs. Answering 5 is the common mistake; each molecule keeps one old strand but also gets a full new partner strand.
column29: Each new molecule is a complete copy of the original.

column9: Mitosis makes two cells that are genetically identical. Which process makes that possible?
column14: DNA replication in S phase makes two identical copies of every chromosome
column15: Transcription makes RNA copies of every gene, which are then split between the two cells
column16: Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm
column17: The cell takes in new DNA from its food
column28: Because replication makes an exact copy of each chromosome, each new cell can get one identical copy. Cytokinesis is a common pick, but it only splits the cytoplasm; it does not copy anything.
column29: Something has to make the copies before they can be shared out.

column9: Which of these cells would be copying its DNA most often?
column14: A mature nerve cell in the brain
column15: A mature human red blood cell
column16: A dead skin cell on the surface of your arm
column17: A cell in the growing tip of a plant root
column28: Root tip cells divide often, and a cell copies its DNA before every division. Mature nerve cells rarely divide, mature human red blood cells have no nucleus, and dead skin cells do nothing at all. Picking the nerve cell because the brain is busy is the common mistake: being active is not the same as dividing.
column29: Cells copy their DNA when they are getting ready to divide. Where is a plant growing fastest?

column9: A section of a template strand reads A T T G C A C. Which new strand will be built on it?
column14: UAACGUG
column15: ATTGCAC
column16: TAACGTG
column17: TAAGCTG
column28: A→T, T→A, T→A, G→C, C→G, A→T, C→G gives TAACGTG. UAACGUG uses U (an RNA base), ATTGCAC copies the template, and TAAGCTG swaps the G and C in the middle.
column29: Work slowly, one base at a time, and check the middle bases twice.

column9: A template strand reads TACGGATC. Type the complete new strand that DNA polymerase builds on it. New strand: ___
column20: ATGCCTAG|A T G C C T A G|A-T-G-C-C-T-A-G|A,T,G,C,C,T,A,G|A, T, G, C, C, T, A, G
column28: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→T, T→A, C→G gives ATGCCTAG. Losing your place in a long strand and skipping a base is a common mistake, so count that you have 8 bases.
column29: Your answer should have the same number of bases as the template.

column9: A newly made strand of DNA reads GATTC. What was the sequence of the template strand it was built on?
column14: GATTC
column15: CTAAG
column16: CUAAG
column17: CTTAG
column28: The new strand is complementary to its template, so work backwards: G→C, A→T, T→A, T→A, C→G gives CTAAG. GATTC repeats the new strand, CUAAG uses U, and CTTAG gets the third base wrong.
column29: Templates and new strands are partners. Find the partner of each base.

column9: One DNA molecule finishes one round of replication. Which statements about the two new molecules are true? Select all that apply.
column14: One of them is made of only new strands
column15: Each one is double-stranded
column16: They have the same base sequence as each other
column17: They contain U wherever the original had T
column18: Each one contains one strand from the original molecule
column28: Each new molecule is double-stranded, has one original strand and one new strand, and has the same sequence as the other. Thinking one copy is all new is the common mistake, and U never goes into DNA.
column29: Think about where each of the two original strands ends up.

column9: Match each replication term to its meaning.
column14: Replication fork :: Y-shaped area where the helix is open and being copied
column15: Semi-conservative :: Each new molecule keeps one strand of the original
column16: Complementary bases :: Partner bases that fit together, like A with T
column17: Nucleotide :: Building block made of a phosphate, a sugar and a base
column18: Double helix :: The twisted-ladder shape of a DNA molecule
column28: The fork is where copying happens, semi-conservative means half saved, complementary bases are partners, nucleotides are the building blocks, and the double helix is the twisted-ladder shape. Mixing up nucleotide and base is a common mistake: a base is only one part of a nucleotide.
column29: Start with the term you are surest of, then use the clue words (Y-shaped, half saved, partners).

column9: In a paper model, the original DNA strands are white and new strands are blue. A student's finished model shows one molecule with two white strands and one molecule with two blue strands. What is wrong with the model?
column14: Each molecule should have one white strand and one blue strand
column15: Each strand should be a mix of white and blue pieces, since old and new DNA get mixed together
column16: Each molecule should have four strands
column17: Nothing is wrong; this is how replication works, since the old strands stay together
column28: Replication is semi-conservative: each old strand stays paired with the new strand built on it, so each molecule is one white and one blue. Two-white plus two-blue is the conservative model, which experiments ruled out.
column29: Each old strand is the template for a new partner. Do they separate after the new strand is built?

column9: Bacteria such as E. coli have no nucleus. Where does their DNA replication take place?
column14: In the nucleus
column15: In the mitochondria
column16: Bacteria do not replicate their DNA
column17: In the cytoplasm
column28: Prokaryotes like E. coli have no nucleus, so their DNA sits in the cytoplasm and is copied there. Answering nucleus is the common mistake of treating every cell like a eukaryotic cell.
column29: If there is no nucleus, where is the DNA kept?

column9: Human chromosomes are very long. How do human cells finish copying them in a reasonable time?
column14: The cell copies only the genes it is using and skips the rest of each chromosome
column15: Helicase skips every other section of DNA
column16: Replication starts at many places along each chromosome at the same time
column17: The cell finishes copying during mitosis
column28: Long eukaryotic chromosomes unzip and copy at many spots at once, and the copied sections join up. Thinking the cell only copies some genes is the common mistake; every base must be copied.
column29: Think of painting a long fence with many painters instead of one.

column9: DNA polymerase fails to fix a mismatched base, and the cell then divides. What is the most likely result?
column14: The DNA in that cell turns into RNA
column15: A mutation is passed to one of the daughter cells
column16: The cell gains an extra chromosome
column17: Nothing, because ligase always fixes wrong bases
column28: An error that is not fixed becomes a permanent change in the base sequence, a mutation, and it is passed on when the cell divides. Ligase only seals gaps between pieces; it does not proofread, which is a common mix-up.
column29: Which enzyme checks for wrong bases? What happens if it misses one?

column9: Put these events in a cell's life in order, starting right after the cell was made.
column14: The cell copies its DNA
column15: The cell makes final preparations to divide
column16: The cell divides by mitosis
column17: The cell grows and does its normal jobs
column28: Grow (G1) → copy DNA (S phase) → prepare (G2) → mitosis. The common mistake is putting DNA copying during or after mitosis, but the DNA must be copied before the chromosomes can be split between two cells.
column29: The copying has to be done before the cell makes its final preparations to divide.

column9: A fruit fly body cell has 8 chromosomes, each made of one DNA molecule. After S phase, how many DNA molecules are in the nucleus? (Enter a number.)
column28: Every chromosome is copied, so each now has two sister chromatids, and each chromatid is one DNA molecule: 8 × 2 = 16. A common mistake is answering 8 by counting chromosomes instead of DNA molecules.
column29: Each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids.

column9: A short piece of DNA has 15 base pairs. How many free nucleotides must DNA polymerase add to build BOTH new strands? (Enter a number.)
column28: Each old strand gets a new 15-base partner, so 15 × 2 = 30 nucleotides. Answering 15 is the common mistake of building only one new strand.
column29: How many new strands are built, and how long is each one?

column9: A template strand is 35% adenine (A). What percent of the new strand built on it will be thymine (T)? (Enter a number.)
column28: Every A on the template gets a T on the new strand, so the new strand is 35% T. A common mistake is answering 15 by thinking A and T must add up to 50%; that rule is about a whole double-stranded molecule, not one strand.
column29: Each A on the template gets exactly one partner on the new strand.

column9: A mutant yeast cell makes a DNA ligase that does not work. What problem would show up in its newly copied DNA?
column14: Some new strands would be left as short, unconnected pieces
column15: The two strands would never separate
column16: Every new base would be wrong
column17: U would be added in place of T
column28: Ligase seals short pieces of new DNA into one strand, so without it those pieces stay disconnected. Saying the strands would not separate is a common mix-up with helicase.
column29: What is ligase's one job?

column9: A drug stops helicase from working in cancer cells. Why would this stop DNA replication?
column14: DNA polymerase would start adding U instead of T, so the copied strand would be RNA
column15: Ligase would start cutting the DNA apart
column16: The cells would make extra copies of their DNA
column17: The strands can't separate, so DNA polymerase can't reach the template bases
column28: With helicase blocked, the helix stays closed and the bases stay paired, so polymerase has nothing to read. Thinking polymerase would switch bases is the common mistake; the problem is access, not the pairing rule.
column29: Which step comes first, and what happens to every later step if it can't happen?

column9: Which statement correctly compares DNA replication with transcription?
column14: Replication copies one gene into new RNA; transcription copies all of the DNA into new DNA
column15: Both processes make proteins directly
column16: Replication copies all of the DNA into new DNA; transcription copies one gene into RNA
column17: Replication uses U and transcription uses T
column28: Replication copies the whole DNA (with T) before a cell divides; transcription copies one gene into RNA (with U). Swapping the two is the common mistake.
column29: Which process makes a second complete set of DNA for a new cell?

column9: What does DNA polymerase need in order to build a new DNA strand? Select all that apply.
column14: A supply of free DNA nucleotides
column15: Sunlight
column16: Ribosomes
column17: An old strand to use as a template
column28: Polymerase reads a template strand and adds free DNA nucleotides. Ribosomes and amino acids are used to build proteins, and uracil nucleotides are for RNA, which are common mix-ups.
column29: Polymerase needs a pattern to follow and the pieces to build with.

column9: A section of DNA has 12 A–T pairs and 8 G–C pairs. After replication, how many G–C pairs will EACH new molecule have? (Enter a number.)
column28: Each new molecule is an exact copy, so each one keeps all 8 G–C pairs. Answering 4 is the common mistake of thinking the pairs are split between the two molecules.
column29: Is each new molecule a full copy or half a copy?

column9: The template strand reads CGATTA. A student writes the new strand as GCTATT. Which base did the student get wrong?
column14: The 1st base; it should be C
column15: The 5th base; it should be A
column16: The 3rd base; it should be A
column17: None; the strand is correct
column28: The correct new strand is GCTAAT. The 5th template base is T, so its partner is A, not T. A common mistake is copying a base instead of pairing it.
column29: Write the correct new strand yourself, then compare it to the student's one base at a time.

column9: Why can either strand of a DNA molecule serve as a template?
column14: Each strand's base sequence decides its partner's sequence through base pairing
column15: The two strands are exactly the same
column16: The enzymes add bases at random, so any strand works as long as it has all four bases
column17: Only one strand is ever copied, so it doesn't matter
column28: Because A pairs with T and C pairs with G, either strand holds all the information needed to rebuild the other. Saying the two strands are the same is the common mistake; they are complementary.
column29: If you know one strand, can you figure out the other?

column9: A tiny piece of DNA has a top strand ATC paired with a bottom strand TAG. Which describes ONE of the molecules after replication?
column14: The old ATC strand paired with a new ATC strand
column15: A new ATC strand paired with a new TAG strand
column16: The old ATC strand paired with a new UAG strand
column17: The old ATC strand paired with a new TAG strand
column28: The old ATC strand is the template, so it gets a new complementary TAG partner. ATC paired with ATC breaks the pairing rule, two new strands breaks the semi-conservative rule, and U never goes in DNA.
column29: Each old strand keeps a new partner that follows the base pairing rule.

column9: During S phase, a cell runs out of free nucleotides that contain guanine (G). Where will building the new strands stall?
column14: Wherever the template strand has a G
column15: Wherever the template strand has an A
column16: Wherever the template strand has a C
column17: Nowhere, because T can be used in place of G
column28: A G must be added across from every C on the template, so polymerase stalls there. Answering G is the common mistake; the G is needed across from C, not across from another G.
column29: Which template base needs a G as its partner?

column9: A template strand has 10 bases: 3 A, 2 T, 4 G and 1 C. How many G's will the new strand have? (Enter a number.)
column28: A G is added across from each C on the template, and there is only 1 C, so the new strand has 1 G. Answering 4 is the common mistake of copying the template's G count instead of pairing.
column29: Which template base gets a G as its partner?

column9: Why does a cell copy its DNA during interphase instead of during mitosis?
column14: DNA cannot be copied inside the nucleus
column15: The chromosomes must already be doubled before mitosis pulls the copies apart
column16: Mitosis destroys the replication enzymes
column17: Cells only need DNA after they divide
column28: Mitosis separates sister chromatids, so the copies have to exist before mitosis begins. Thinking the copying happens while chromosomes are being pulled apart is the common mistake.
column29: What does mitosis split up, and where did those copies come from?

column9: A student looking at an onion root tip under the microscope sees a cell whose chromosomes are each made of two sister chromatids. What does this tell her?
column14: The cell has already replicated its DNA
column15: The cell has not replicated its DNA yet
column16: The cell is making RNA from its genes
column17: The cell has a mutation
column28: Two sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies made in S phase, so this cell has replicated. Thinking doubled chromosomes mean a mutation is a common mistake; it is the normal result of replication.
column29: Where do sister chromatids come from?

column9: A student's notes on DNA replication contain several claims. Select every claim that is correct.
column14: The new strand is identical to its template strand
column15: Uracil pairs with adenine in the new DNA
column16: Replication happens before the cell divides
column17: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases
column19: DNA polymerase checks for and fixes many of its own mistakes
column28: Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds, polymerase proofreads, and replication comes before division. The new strand is complementary to its template, not identical; ligase seals pieces instead of unzipping; and U is only in RNA.
column29: Check each claim against the job of each enzyme and the base pairing rule.

column9: Erwin Chargaff found that in DNA the amount of A equals the amount of T, and C equals G. Why does every copy made by replication still follow this rule?
column14: Replication adds extra A and T to keep the numbers even
column15: Replication copies only the A–T pairs
column16: The rule only applies to the original molecule, not the copies, because copies are built from new bases
column17: Each A on a template gets a T partner and each C gets a G, so every copy has matched pairs
column28: Base pairing builds the new strand from matched partners, so every copy has equal A and T and equal C and G. Thinking the cell has to add extra bases to balance things out is the common mistake.
column29: Think about how each base on the new strand is chosen.

column9: A section of a human gene has the template strand AGGTCCA. Type the new strand that forms on it during replication. New strand: ___
column20: TCCAGGT|T C C A G G T|T-C-C-A-G-G-T|T,C,C,A,G,G,T|T, C, C, A, G, G, T
column28: A→T, G→C, G→C, T→A, C→G, C→G, A→T gives TCCAGGT. Mixing up the C–G pairs in the middle is the common mistake, so check those bases twice.
column29: Count your bases: the new strand has the same length as the template.

column9: A photocopier copies a page and leaves the original page untouched. How is DNA replication different from a photocopier?
column14: DNA replication makes a mirror-image opposite of the whole molecule and leaves the original whole
column15: DNA replication makes RNA instead of DNA
column16: Each new DNA molecule keeps one strand of the original instead of leaving the original whole
column17: There is no difference; the original stays whole
column28: In replication the original molecule is split, and each half is kept in one of the new molecules (semi-conservative). Saying the original stays whole is the common mistake.
column29: After replication, is there still a complete "original" molecule anywhere?

column9: A DNA molecule has a top strand and a bottom strand. During replication, a new strand is built on the top strand. The new strand will have the same base sequence as which strand?
column14: The original top strand
column15: The original bottom strand
column16: Neither original strand
column17: Half of the top strand and half of the bottom strand
column28: The new strand is complementary to the top strand, and so is the original bottom strand, so the new strand matches the bottom strand base for base. Choosing the top strand is the common mistake; a new strand is never identical to its own template.
column29: Which original strand was already the partner of the top strand?

column9: Put the detailed steps of DNA replication in order.
column14: DNA ligase seals the gaps between pieces of new DNA
column15: DNA polymerase adds matching nucleotides to build the new strands
column16: The two finished DNA molecules twist back into double helices
column17: Primase lays down a short primer
column18: Helicase unzips the DNA at a starting point, opening a replication fork
column28: Unzip → primer → build → seal → twist. A common mistake is putting polymerase before primase, but polymerase cannot start a new strand without a primer to add onto.
column29: Polymerase can only add to something that is already there.

column9: Scientists grew bacteria in food with "heavy" nitrogen until all of their DNA was heavy. Then they moved the bacteria to food with normal "light" nitrogen and let them replicate ONE time. If replication is semi-conservative, what should the new DNA look like?
column14: Every molecule has one heavy strand and one light strand
column15: Half the molecules are all heavy and half are all light
column16: Every molecule is all heavy
column17: Every molecule is all light
column28: Each heavy original strand stays and pairs with a new light strand, so every molecule is half heavy and half light. Half all-heavy and half all-light is what the conservative model predicts, which is the common mistake.
column29: The old strands are heavy; the new strands are built from the light food.

column9: In the same heavy/light nitrogen experiment, the bacteria replicate a SECOND time in light-nitrogen food. If replication is semi-conservative, what should the DNA look like now?
column14: Every molecule is a heavy-light hybrid
column15: Half the molecules are all heavy and half are all light
column16: A quarter are all heavy, half are hybrids and a quarter are all light
column17: Half the molecules are heavy-light hybrids and half are all light
column28: After round 1, each molecule is heavy + light. In round 2, each heavy strand gets a light partner (hybrid) and each light strand gets a light partner (all light), so it is half hybrid and half all light. Thinking all-heavy DNA comes back is the common mistake; no step ever pairs two heavy strands again.
column29: Follow each of the four strands from round 1 and give each one a new light partner.

column9: Scientists once tested the idea that the original DNA molecule stays whole and a completely new molecule is built beside it. In the heavy/light nitrogen experiment, DNA spun in a tube forms bands by weight. If that idea were true, what would scientists see after ONE round of replication in light-nitrogen food?
column14: One band halfway between heavy and light
column15: Only an all-heavy band
column16: One all-heavy band and one all-light band
column17: Only an all-light band
column28: If the original stayed whole, it would still be all heavy, and the brand-new molecule would be all light, so there would be two separate bands. A band halfway between is the common wrong pick: that is what you get when every molecule has one heavy and one light strand, which is the semi-conservative result.
column29: Under this idea, which molecule is made only of old (heavy) strands, and which only of new (light) ones?

column9: One DNA molecule is placed in a test tube with everything needed for replication and is copied for 3 rounds (every molecule copies itself each round). How many DNA molecules are there at the end? (Enter a number.)
column28: The number doubles each round: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. A common mistake is answering 6 by adding 2 each round instead of doubling.
column29: Each molecule present at the start of a round becomes two.

column9: One DNA molecule replicates for 4 rounds. How many of the molecules at the end still contain one of the two original strands? (Enter a number.)
column28: The two original strands are never broken up or copied away; each stays in one molecule, paired with a new strand. So of the 16 molecules, exactly 2 contain an original strand, no matter how many rounds. Answering 16 or 8 is the common mistake of thinking the old strands get split among the copies.
column29: Follow the two original strands. Do they ever get broken into pieces?

column9: One DNA molecule replicates for 3 rounds. What percent of all the DNA strands at the end are original strands? (Enter a number.)
column28: Count strands, not molecules: 3 rounds make 8 molecules, which is 16 strands. Only 2 strands are original, and 2 ÷ 16 = 0.125 = 12.5%. A common mistake is using 2 ÷ 8 = 25% by counting molecules.
column29: First find the number of molecules, then the number of strands (two per molecule).

column9: A dog body cell has 78 chromosomes. The cell replicates its DNA and then divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes does EACH daughter cell have? (Enter a number.)
column28: Replication doubles the DNA to 78 pairs of sister chromatids, and mitosis splits them so each daughter cell gets 78 chromosomes, the same as the parent. Answering 156 is the common mistake of forgetting that mitosis divides the copies.
column29: Replication makes copies, and mitosis shares them out. Compare each daughter to the parent.

column9: An E. coli chromosome has about 4,600,000 base pairs. Replication starts at one origin, and two replication forks move away from it in opposite directions, each copying about 1,000 base pairs per second. About how many seconds does it take to copy the whole chromosome? (Enter a number.)
column28: The two forks share the work, so together they copy 2,000 base pairs per second: 4,600,000 ÷ 2,000 = 2,300 seconds (about 38 minutes). Answering 4,600 is the common mistake of using only one fork.
column29: How many base pairs per second do both forks copy together?

column9: A chromosome has 6,000,000 base pairs. Replication starts at 60 evenly spaced starting points, and each starting point opens two forks that each copy 50 base pairs per second. About how many seconds does the whole chromosome take? (Enter a number.)
column28: Each starting point handles 6,000,000 ÷ 60 = 100,000 base pairs. Its two forks split that, so each fork copies 50,000 base pairs at 50 per second: 1,000 seconds. Forgetting the second fork (giving 2,000) is the common mistake.
column29: Split the chromosome among the starting points first, then split each section between two forks.

column9: DNA polymerase can build a new strand in only one direction. What is the result at each replication fork?
column14: Both new strands are built in one continuous piece
column15: One new strand is built in one continuous piece, and the other is built in short pieces
column16: Only one of the two old strands gets copied
column17: Both new strands are built backward and then flipped around so they face the same direction
column28: Because polymerase works in one direction and the strands face opposite ways, the leading strand is continuous and the lagging strand is made in short pieces (Okazaki fragments). Thinking one old strand is skipped is the common mistake; both must be copied.
column29: The two old strands run in opposite directions, but polymerase can only go one way.

column9: What are Okazaki fragments?
column14: Short pieces of new DNA made on the lagging strand
column15: Pieces of RNA that leave the nucleus to make proteins
column16: Broken pieces of the old strand that get thrown away
column17: Mistakes left behind by DNA polymerase
column28: Okazaki fragments are the short stretches of new DNA built on the lagging strand, later joined by ligase. Thinking they are broken old DNA is the common mistake; the old strand stays whole.
column29: These fragments are what DNA ligase joins together.

column9: Why does DNA replication need primase?
column14: Primase unzips the double helix
column15: Primase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments
column16: Primase removes the wrong bases that polymerase adds, so the new strand matches the template exactly
column17: DNA polymerase can't start a strand from nothing, so primase makes a short primer to build on
column28: Primase builds a short primer that gives DNA polymerase a starting point. The distractors describe helicase, ligase and polymerase proofreading, which is the usual mix-up.
column29: Think of a primer coat of paint: it goes on first so the next layer has something to stick to.

column9: Select every statement that is true about the lagging strand. Select all that apply.
column14: It is made of RNA instead of DNA
column15: It is built in many short pieces
column16: It is only found in bacteria
column17: It needs DNA ligase to join its pieces
column18: It is built in one long continuous piece
column19: It needs more than one primer, one for each piece
column28: The lagging strand is made in short pieces (Okazaki fragments), each started by its own primer and later sealed by ligase. It is still DNA, and it happens in every cell that copies DNA. Describing it as continuous mixes it up with the leading strand.
column29: Think about what it takes to make a strand out of many short pieces instead of one long one.

column9: A scientist measures the DNA in one cell. In G1 it has 6 units of DNA. How much DNA does it have at the end of S phase, and how much does each daughter cell have after mitosis?
column14: 12 units at the end of S phase, and 12 units in each daughter cell
column15: 6 units at the end of S phase, and 3 units in each daughter cell
column16: 12 units at the end of S phase, and 6 units in each daughter cell
column17: 3 units at the end of S phase, and 6 units in each daughter cell
column28: Replication doubles the DNA (6 → 12), and mitosis splits it evenly so each daughter has 6, the same as the parent in G1. Keeping 12 in each daughter is the common mistake of forgetting that the copies get divided.
column29: S phase makes copies. Mitosis shares the copies between two cells.

column9: A classmate says: "After replication, the two DNA molecules are complementary to each other, like a strand and its partner." Which correction is best?
column14: The claim is correct as written
column15: The two molecules are identical to each other; it is the two strands inside each molecule that are complementary
column16: The two molecules are completely different from each other
column17: Each molecule is identical to only one strand of the original
column28: Replication makes two identical double-stranded molecules. Complementary describes the two strands within one molecule. Mixing up strands and molecules is the core mistake in the claim.
column29: Separate the idea of a strand (one side) from a molecule (both sides together).

column9: A double-stranded DNA molecule is 30% adenine (A). After it replicates, what percent of each new molecule will be guanine (G)? (Enter a number.)
column28: The copies match the original. If A = 30%, then T = 30%, so A + T = 60% and G + C = 40%. Since G = C, G = 20%. A common mistake is answering 70 by subtracting A from 100 without accounting for T.
column29: Find T first, then split what is left equally between G and C.

column9: A template strand reads TGACCTAG. A new strand is built on it. Then, in the next round of replication, that NEW strand is used as a template. Type the strand that is built in the second round. Second-round strand: ___
column20: TGACCTAG|T G A C C T A G|T-G-A-C-C-T-A-G|T,G,A,C,C,T,A,G|T, G, A, C, C, T, A, G
column28: Round 1 builds ACTGGATC on TGACCTAG. Round 2 pairs each base of ACTGGATC again, which gives TGACCTAG, the same as the first template. Stopping after round 1 is the common mistake.
column29: Build the first new strand, then build a partner for that one.

column9: During replication, polymerase puts a G across from a T on the template by mistake, and it is not fixed. The molecule replicates again. What is true about the two molecules made in that second round?
column14: One has the normal A–T pair at that spot, and the other has a G–C pair, so the change is now permanent
column15: Both molecules automatically get fixed back to A–T
column16: Both molecules have the G–T mismatch
column17: The mistake disappears because mismatched bases cannot be copied
column28: In round 2 the strands separate. The old T strand gets an A (normal T–A pair), and the strand with the wrong G gets a C, giving a G–C pair. That G–C pair follows the pairing rule, so the cell can't spot it, and it is now a mutation. Thinking both copies keep the mismatch is the common mistake.
column29: Separate the two strands and give each one the partner the pairing rule calls for.

column9: A drug blocks an enzyme that bacteria need to copy their DNA, but it does not affect human cells. Why does this drug stop a bacterial infection from spreading?
column14: The bacteria can't make energy from food
column15: The drug kills the human cells around the bacteria, so the bacteria have nowhere left to live
column16: The bacteria start making RNA instead of DNA
column17: The bacteria can't copy their DNA, so they can't divide to make more bacteria
column28: Bacteria must replicate their DNA before each division, so blocking replication stops them from multiplying. Thinking the drug hurts human cells is the common mistake; it targets only the bacterial enzyme.
column29: What has to happen before any cell can divide?

column9: A model of a replication fork shows one new strand as one long piece. The other new strand is several short pieces with small gaps between them, and the primers have already been replaced with DNA. Which enzyme must act next on the strand with gaps?
column14: Helicase
column15: Primase
column16: DNA ligase
column17: RNA polymerase
column28: The pieces are built and the primers replaced, so the only job left is sealing the gaps, which is ligase's job. Picking primase is the common mistake; primase starts pieces, it does not connect them. RNA polymerase is for transcription.
column29: The pieces are already built. What is left to do?

column9: Each problem below is caused by one replication enzyme that is not working. Match each problem to that enzyme.
column14: The two strands never come apart :: Helicase
column15: No new strand can get started because there is no starting point :: Primase
column16: Wrong bases are added and never fixed :: DNA polymerase
column17: The lagging strand stays in disconnected pieces :: DNA ligase
column28: Helicase separates strands, primase makes starter primers, DNA polymerase builds and proofreads, and ligase connects pieces. Blaming ligase for wrong bases is the common mistake; checking bases is polymerase's job.
column29: Ask which enzyme normally does the job that is failing.

column9: Think of DNA as a twisted ladder. During replication, which bonds are broken and which new bonds are made?
column14: Sugar-phosphate bonds in the old backbone break; nothing new is formed, since the old strands are reused
column15: Hydrogen bonds between bases break; new hydrogen bonds and new sugar-phosphate bonds form
column16: No bonds are broken, because the new strand is built on the outside of the ladder
column17: Peptide bonds break and new peptide bonds form between bases
column28: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds in the rungs, the old backbones stay whole, and polymerase connects new nucleotides by their sugar-phosphate backbone while each new base hydrogen-bonds to its old partner. Thinking the old backbone breaks is the common mistake.
column29: The rails of the ladder stay whole. What holds the rungs together?

column9: A student builds a model of a replication fork. Select every feature the model SHOULD show. Select all that apply.
column14: U bases in the new strands
column15: The two old strands zipped back together behind the fork
column16: Helicase at the point where the two strands separate
column17: Each old strand paired with a growing new strand
column18: Short pieces of new DNA on one of the new strands
column28: A correct fork shows helicase opening the strands, each old strand acting as a template for a new strand, and Okazaki fragments on the lagging side. Zipping the old strands back together is the common mistake; each old strand stays with its new partner (semi-conservative).
column29: Picture the Y shape: what is at the point of the Y, and what is on each arm?

column9: In an experiment, a cell's DNA polymerase loses its ability to proofread but can still build strands. What would most likely happen over many cell divisions?
column14: Mutations would build up much faster in the cell's descendants
column15: Replication would stop completely, since the polymerase could no longer work
column16: The cell's DNA would turn into RNA
column17: The daughter cells would have fewer chromosomes, because some would be left uncopied
column28: Polymerase can still copy, so replication continues, but the mistakes it normally fixes would stay and be passed on, so mutations pile up. Thinking replication would stop is the common mistake; building and proofreading are separate abilities.
column29: The enzyme can still build. What extra job did it lose?
